It\n4\tcontains instructions on how a commit cycle accomplished.\n5\t\n6\t## Cycles\n7\t\n8\tA cycle has three phases:\n9\t\n10\t- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's\n11\t  first commit. Sets up the cycle:\n12\t  - Backfill the previous cycle's chores `Commits:` ref.\n13\t  - Bump `Cargo.toml` to `X.Y.Z-0`.\n14\t  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,\n15\t    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem\n16\t    statement + plan ladder).\n17\t  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).\n18\t- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the\n19\t  commits that implement the change. As many as the change\n20\t  needs; each runs through the\n21\t  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).\n22\t- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's\n23\t  last commit. Bookkeeping only:\n24\t  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in\n25\t    `## Done`.\n26\t  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the\n27\t    [chores section](#chores-sections).\n28\t  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality\n29\t    changed.\n30\t\n31\tA cycle's commits are published to the project remote\n32\teither incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the\n33\tresult must always be published at close-out. See\n34\t[Pushing](#pushing).\n35\t\n36\t**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to\n37\twarrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`\n38\tPreparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`\n39\tClose-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively\n40\tat every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the\n41\tsuffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)\n42\tfor the local-ladder mechanics.\n43\t\n44\t## Chores sections\n45\t\n46\tA **chores section** is a `##` section in\n47\t`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording one cycle:\n48\t\n49\t- One section per cycle is the default.\n50\t- Per-commit sections (like 0.55.0's four) are a\n51\t  deliberate alternative.\n52\t\n53\tThe phrase **\"Open\" the chores section** means append a\n54\t`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`\n55\twith the cycle's anticipated close-out title (e.g.\n56\t`## refactor: foo bar (X.Y.Z)`). The body is empty;\n57\tcontent arrives at close-out (see [Close-out](#close-out)).\n58\t\n59\tFuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,\n60\tdesign subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in\n61\tAGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).\n62\t\n63\t## Preparation\n64\t\n65\tThe cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`):\n66\t\n67\t- **Backfill the previous cycle's chores section\n68\t  `Commits:` ref** — see\n69\t  [Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references).\n70\t- **Bump the version** in `Cargo.toml` to `X.Y.Z-0`.\n71\t- **Update `Cargo.lock`** to match — run `cargo build`\n72\t  (or `cargo check`) so the lockfile's `vc-x1` version\n73\t  tracks `Cargo.toml` in the same commit.\n74\t- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into\n75\t  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:\n76\t  - A **bold title line** — that will be the chores\n77\t    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.\n78\t  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed\n79\t  - A **plan ladder**.\n80\t- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)** —\n81\t  append a `##` header with the cycle's anticipated\n82\t  close-out title.\n83\t\n84\t## Work-N\n85\t\n86\tThe cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …)\n87\timplement the change. As many as needed:\n88\t\n89\t- Each commit runs through the\n90\t  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.\n91\t- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress\n92\t  visibility).\n93\t- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see\n94\t  [Pushing](#pushing)).\n95\t- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's\n96\t  scope grows enough (see\n97\t  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).\n98\t\n99\t## Close-out\n100\t\n101\tThe cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping\n102\tonly — the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not\n103\twhat happens post-squash:\n104\t\n105\t- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a\n106\t  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.\n107\t- **Move the `## In Progress` block into the\n108\t  [chores section](#chores-sections)** (the title-only\n109\t  placeholder opened during Preparation):\n110\t  - Cut the problem statement + plan ladder out of\n111\t    `## In Progress` (drop the bold title line — the\n112\t    chores `##` header already carries that string).\n113\t  - Paste under the chores `##` header.\n114\t  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title\n115\t    if the cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor\n116\t    back-reference.\n117\t  - Add an `### As-built ladder` listing the cycle's\n118\t    commits; optional `### Outcome` notes.\n119\t  - Replace `## In Progress` with\n120\t    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.\n121\t- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed\n122\t  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).\n123\t\n124\tWhether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the\n125\tpublishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time —\n126\tsee [Pushing](#pushing).\n127\t\n128\t## Numbering\n129\t\n130\tThe version suffix on each commit encodes its phase —\n131\tthe **final identifier `0` marks a Preparation**:\n132\t\n133\t- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation\n134\t- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits\n135\t- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)\n136\t\n137\tDisambiguation:\n138\t\n139\t- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a\n140\t  Preparation.\n141\t- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final\n142\t  identifier `0`).\n143\t\n144\t**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:\n145\t\n146\t- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle\n147\t- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work\n148\t- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out\n149\t- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle\n150\t\n151\tSub-cycles needing no Preparation omit `.0` (`-3.1`,\n152\t`-3.2`, `-3`); one that grows a Preparation later adds\n153\t`-3.0` without renumbering siblings.\n154\t\n155\tBump `Cargo.toml` at the start of each phase so `vc-x1 -V`\n156\treports the active phase at build time.\n157\t\n158\t## Per-commit flow\n159\t\n160\tEvery commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes\n161\tthrough:\n162\t\n163\t1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in\n164\t   `notes/todo.md > ## In Progress`.\n165\t2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)\n166\t   for the loop-and-squash technique).\n167\t3. **Flip this commit `(current)` → `(done)`** in `## In\n168\t   Progress` — before the cargo cycle and the commit.\n169\t4. **Cargo cycle** (skip-able for purely-docs commits; full\n170\t   cycle mandatory at close-out):\n171\t   1. `cargo fmt`\n172\t   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`\n173\t   3. `cargo test`\n174\t   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`\n175\t   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)\n176\t5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;\n177\t   tell the user \"ready to commit.\" The user reviews the\n178\t   changes and we iterate until complete.\n179\t6. **Write the commit description** — see\n180\t   [Commit description](#commit-description).\n181\t7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body\n182\t   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.\n183\t8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m \"title\" -m \"body\" -R .` for\n184\t   the app repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last\n185\t   keeps the verb visible):\n186\t\n187\t   ```\n188\t   jj commit -m \\\n189\t   \"<type>: <short description> (<version>)\" \\\n190\t   -m \"<intro paragraph>\n191\t\n192\t   - file1: gist\n193\t   - file2: gist\n194\t\n195\t   ochid: /.claude/<chid>\" \\\n196\t   -R .\n197\t   ```\n198\t\n199\t**Two overrides apply:**\n200\t\n201\t- **Deviation or question** — any time the work deviates\n202\t  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and\n203\t  surface it; don't push through.\n204\t- **ESC-ESC** — the user can interrupt at any point to pull\n205\t  a review or question forward.\n206\t\n207\t## Commit description\n208\t\n209\t[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)\n210\twith a version suffix:\n211\t\n212\t```\n213\t<type>: <short description> (<version>)\n214\t```\n215\t\n216\t### Title\n217\t\n218\t- ≤50 chars total (version suffix counts).\n219\t- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,\n220\t  `docs`, `chore`.\n221\t- Favor terse phrasings.\n222\t\n223\t### Body\n224\t\n225\t[Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),\n226\twrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:\n227\t\n228\t- **App-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file\n229\t  changed (file plus a one-line gist). Sub-bullets for\n230\t  files with multiple distinct changes:\n231\t\n232\t  ```\n233\t  - path/to/file1\n234\t    - first distinct change\n235\t    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line\n236\t       with continuation indented 5\n237\t  ```\n238\t\n239\t  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the\n240\t  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the\n241\t  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any\n242\t  \"why\" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.\n243\t\n244\t- **Session-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe\n245\t  in-session activity rather than code changes.\n246\t\n247\t### Trailer\n248\t\n249\t`ochid:` as the last line of the body — see\n250\t[ochid trailers](#ochid-trailers).\n251\t\n252\t## Reviewing changes\n253\t\n254\tWork review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,\n255\ton the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their\n256\teditor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:\n257\t\n258\t- `jj diff` — working-copy diff (uncommitted)\n259\t- `jj diff -r @-` — diff of the previous commit\n260\t- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>` — any two revisions\n261\t- `jj show -r <X>` — description + diff for one rev\n262\t\n263\tDon't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit — that marks\n264\tit mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or\n265\t`jj show -r @-`.\n266\t\n267\tSee [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the\n268\tclose-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives\n269\tare in [`jj-revsets.md`](jj-revsets.md).\n270\t\n271\t## Pushing\n272\t\n273\t### Policy\n274\t\n275\tPush is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,\n276\tprogress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out** —\n277\tthe cycle's result must be published.\n278\t\n279\t### Shape at close-out push\n280\t\n281\tAt close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published\n282\tshape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface\n283\tthe options and get user approval before pushing — once on\n284\tthe target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,\n285\tneeds approval), so choose deliberately.\n286\t\n287\t- **Squash to one commit** — single entry on the target.\n288\t  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is\n289\t  focused on one or two files.\n290\t- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)* — `main` gains a\n291\t  merge commit (`X.Y.Z`); cycle commits stay reachable via\n292\t  two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal\n293\t  shape. See [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe)\n294\t  for the full setup sequence.\n295\t- **Keep separate** — one commit per cycle entry on\n296\t  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is\n297\t  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /\n298\t  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.\n299\t\n300\tSet up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use\n301\t`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.\n302\t\n303\t### Merge non-ff recipe\n304\t\n305\tSetting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)\n306\tclose-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's\n307\tclose-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out\n308\t(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last\n309\tWork commit:\n310\t\n311\t1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r\n312\t   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.\n313\t   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.\n314\t   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).\n315\t   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.\n316\t\n317\t   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of\n318\t   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.\n319\t2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the\n320\t   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing\n321\t   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;\n322\t   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.\n323\t3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.\n324\t\n325\t**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed\n326\t[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are\n327\timmutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the\n328\tpush force-updates `main`.\n329\tThe standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*\n330\tthe close-out push.\n331\t\n332\t### vc-x1 push wrapper\n333\t\n334\t`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See\n335\t`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags.\n336\t\n337\t**Current limitation**: only fully supports the\n338\t[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other\n339\tshapes need manual jj steps. Improvements tracked /\n340\tplanned:\n341\t\n342\t- N:1 code↔bot for Merge non-ff (`## Todo` entry P1).\n343\t- Symmetric squash (planned, to be captured in `-2`).\n344\t- Per-repo bookmark names (planned).\n345\t\n346\t### .claude cadence\n347\t\n348\t**Cadence**: one push = one `.claude` commit, paired\n349\twith every code commit in that push.\n350\t\n351\tThe `.claude` working copy accumulates session data\n352\tacross the cycle; its change ID stays stable across\n353\tsnapshots, `jj describe`, and the finalize commit, so\n354\tcode-side `ochid:` trailers resolve.\n355\t\n356\t`.claude` is a linear journal — all session work lives\n357\ton `main`, regardless of the app-side bookmark. **Do not\n358\tcreate or maintain `.claude` bookmarks that mirror\n359\tapp-side branches** — risks the bot steering session\n360\tpushes to the wrong remote ref.\n361\t\n362\tEnding a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be\n363\tsession information created, which we don't worry about.\n364\tThe user can close the terminal instead and `@` will\n365\tremain empty — this behavior was verified in 0.64.0.\n366\t\n367\t### Bot communication at the reviews\n368\t\n369\tUse plain prose — no insider jargon (\"Gate N signal\",\n370\t\"Checkpoint N\", etc.):\n371\t\n372\t- **At Work review** — summarize what changed and stop.\n373\t  \"Work complete. Please review.\"\n374\t- **At Commit Description review** — present `$TITLE`\n375\t  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.\n376\t  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...\n377\t  --body ...` invocation by default.\n378\t- **At Post close-out review** — surface the shape\n379\t  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;\n380\t  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /\n381\t  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.\n382\t\n383\t### After push or finalize: stop and wait\n384\t\n385\tAfter you **push** (cross the remote boundary) or launch\n386\t**finalize** on the `.claude` repo (`vc-x1 finalize --repo\n387\t.claude --squash --push <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach`) — by\n388\thand or via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper — you **MUST NEVER**\n389\tproceed (next step, edit, tool call, text output) until the\n390\tuser explicitly directs you to continue. **Even when the next\n391\tstep seems obvious — wait.** Treat push-or-finalize as a hard\n392\tstop for the whole turn.\n393\t\n394\t`vc-x1 push` performs both as its tail stages — `push-app`\n395\tthen the detached `vc-x1 finalize` on `.claude` — so there is\n396\tno gap left to speak in once the push is invoked. Put **all**\n397\tclosing words *before* invoking it; do not purposely emit anything\n398\tafter the tool returns.\n399\t\n400\tWhy (`.claude` is the live journal finalize snapshots →\n401\tsquashes → pushes):\n402\t\n403\t- **`--detach`**: lets the tool return immediately so the\n404\t  harness can keep flushing the *trailing* session-data — the\n405\t  tool call's own transcript and any words emitted *before*\n406\t  the invoke — into the snapshot.\n407\t- **`--delay 10`**: gives the harness time to complete that\n408\t  flush before the snapshot is taken. It is **not** time for\n409\t  the bot to do more work.\n410\t- **silence**: the bot must not summarize or perform any work\n411\t  after the tool returns.\n412\t\n413\t**Known slip**: the bot has emitted a summary after launching\n414\tfinalize. There is no \"harmless\" closing line — if it's worth\n415\tsaying, say it *before* the invoke.\n416\t\n417\t### Recovery\n418\t\n419\t- **If push exits before `finalize-claude`** (e.g.\n420\t  failure between `push-app` and `finalize-claude`), run\n421\t  finalize by hand:\n422\t\n423\t  ```\n424\t  vc-x1 finalize --repo .claude --squash --push <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach --log /tmp/vc-x1-finalize.log\n425\t  ```\n426\t\n427\t- **Run finalize again if `@` is non-empty** after the\n428\t  finalize's squash-and-commit (also desirable after\n429\t  extra activity by the bot's agents).\n430\t  - Why: finalize snapshots `.claude` at `--delay`, but the\n431\t    bot keeps writing session data while it runs — the tool's\n432\t    own invocation plus the bot's closing response land\n433\t    *after* the snapshot.\n434\t  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a\n435\t    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. It\ncontains instructions on how a commit cycle accomplished.\n\n## Cycles\n\nA cycle has three phases:\n\n- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's\n  first commit. Sets up the cycle:\n  - Backfill the previous cycle's chores `Commits:` ref.\n  - Bump `Cargo.toml` to `X.Y.Z-0`.\n  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,\n    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem\n    statement + plan ladder).\n  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).\n- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the\n  commits that implement the change. As many as the change\n  needs; each runs through the\n  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).\n- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's\n  last commit. Bookkeeping only:\n  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in\n    `## Done`.\n  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the\n    [chores section](#chores-sections).\n  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality\n    changed.\n\nA cycle's commits are published to the project remote\neither incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the\nresult must always be published at close-out. See\n[Pushing](#pushing).\n\n**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to\nwarrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`\nPreparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`\nClose-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively\nat every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the\nsuffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)\nfor the local-ladder mechanics.\n\n## Chores sections\n\nA **chores section** is a `##` section in\n`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording one cycle:\n\n- One section per cycle is the default.\n- Per-commit sections (like 0.55.0's four) are a\n  deliberate alternative.\n\nThe phrase **\"Open\" the chores section** means append a\n`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`\nwith the cycle's anticipated close-out title (e.g.\n`## refactor: foo bar (X.Y.Z)`). The body is empty;\ncontent arrives at close-out (see [Close-out](#close-out)).\n\nFuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,\ndesign subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in\nAGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).\n\n## Preparation\n\nThe cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`):\n\n- **Backfill the previous cycle's chores section\n  `Commits:` ref** — see\n  [Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references).\n- **Bump the version** in `Cargo.toml` to `X.Y.Z-0`.\n- **Update `Cargo.lock`** to match — run `cargo build`\n  (or `cargo check`) so the lockfile's `vc-x1` version\n  tracks `Cargo.toml` in the same commit.\n- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into\n  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:\n  - A **bold title line** — that will be the chores\n    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.\n  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed\n  - A **plan ladder**.\n- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)** —\n  append a `##` header with the cycle's anticipated\n  close-out title.\n\n## Work-N\n\nThe cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …)\nimplement the change. As many as needed:\n\n- Each commit runs through the\n  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.\n- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress\n  visibility).\n- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see\n  [Pushing](#pushing)).\n- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's\n  scope grows enough (see\n  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).\n\n## Close-out\n\nThe cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping\nonly — the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not\nwhat happens post-squash:\n\n- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a\n  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.\n- **Move the `## In Progress` block into the\n  [chores section](#chores-sections)** (the title-only\n  placeholder opened during Preparation):\n  - Cut the problem statement + plan ladder out of\n    `## In Progress` (drop the bold title line — the\n    chores `##` header already carries that string).\n  - Paste under the chores `##` header.\n  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title\n    if the cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor\n    back-reference.\n  - Add an `### As-built ladder` listing the cycle's\n    commits; optional `### Outcome` notes.\n  - Replace `## In Progress` with\n    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.\n- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed\n  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).\n\nWhether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the\npublishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time —\nsee [Pushing](#pushing).\n\n## Numbering\n\nThe version suffix on each commit encodes its phase —\nthe **final identifier `0` marks a Preparation**:\n\n- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation\n- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits\n- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)\n\nDisambiguation:\n\n- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a\n  Preparation.\n- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final\n  identifier `0`).\n\n**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:\n\n- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle\n- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work\n- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out\n- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle\n\nSub-cycles needing no Preparation omit `.0` (`-3.1`,\n`-3.2`, `-3`); one that grows a Preparation later adds\n`-3.0` without renumbering siblings.\n\nBump `Cargo.toml` at the start of each phase so `vc-x1 -V`\nreports the active phase at build time.\n\n## Per-commit flow\n\nEvery commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes\nthrough:\n\n1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in\n   `notes/todo.md > ## In Progress`.\n2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)\n   for the loop-and-squash technique).\n3. **Flip this commit `(current)` → `(done)`** in `## In\n   Progress` — before the cargo cycle and the commit.\n4. **Cargo cycle** (skip-able for purely-docs commits; full\n   cycle mandatory at close-out):\n   1. `cargo fmt`\n   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`\n   3. `cargo test`\n   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`\n   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)\n5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;\n   tell the user \"ready to commit.\" The user reviews the\n   changes and we iterate until complete.\n6. **Write the commit description** — see\n   [Commit description](#commit-description).\n7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body\n   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.\n8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m \"title\" -m \"body\" -R .` for\n   the app repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last\n   keeps the verb visible):\n\n   ```\n   jj commit -m \\\n   \"<type>: <short description> (<version>)\" \\\n   -m \"<intro paragraph>\n\n   - file1: gist\n   - file2: gist\n\n   ochid: /.claude/<chid>\" \\\n   -R .\n   ```\n\n**Two overrides apply:**\n\n- **Deviation or question** — any time the work deviates\n  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and\n  surface it; don't push through.\n- **ESC-ESC** — the user can interrupt at any point to pull\n  a review or question forward.\n\n## Commit description\n\n[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)\nwith a version suffix:\n\n```\n<type>: <short description> (<version>)\n```\n\n### Title\n\n- ≤50 chars total (version suffix counts).\n- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,\n  `docs`, `chore`.\n- Favor terse phrasings.\n\n### Body\n\n[Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),\nwrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:\n\n- **App-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file\n  changed (file plus a one-line gist). Sub-bullets for\n  files with multiple distinct changes:\n\n  ```\n  - path/to/file1\n    - first distinct change\n    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line\n       with continuation indented 5\n  ```\n\n  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the\n  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the\n  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any\n  \"why\" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.\n\n- **Session-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe\n  in-session activity rather than code changes.\n\n### Trailer\n\n`ochid:` as the last line of the body — see\n[ochid trailers](#ochid-trailers).\n\n## Reviewing changes\n\nWork review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,\non the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their\neditor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:\n\n- `jj diff` — working-copy diff (uncommitted)\n- `jj diff -r @-` — diff of the previous commit\n- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>` — any two revisions\n- `jj show -r <X>` — description + diff for one rev\n\nDon't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit — that marks\nit mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or\n`jj show -r @-`.\n\nSee [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the\nclose-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives\nare in [`jj-revsets.md`](jj-revsets.md).\n\n## Pushing\n\n### Policy\n\nPush is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,\nprogress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out** —\nthe cycle's result must be published.\n\n### Shape at close-out push\n\nAt close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published\nshape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface\nthe options and get user approval before pushing — once on\nthe target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,\nneeds approval), so choose deliberately.\n\n- **Squash to one commit** — single entry on the target.\n  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is\n  focused on one or two files.\n- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)* — `main` gains a\n  merge commit (`X.Y.Z`); cycle commits stay reachable via\n  two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal\n  shape. See [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe)\n  for the full setup sequence.\n- **Keep separate** — one commit per cycle entry on\n  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is\n  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /\n  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.\n\nSet up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use\n`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.\n\n### Merge non-ff recipe\n\nSetting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)\nclose-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's\nclose-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out\n(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last\nWork commit:\n\n1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r\n   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.\n   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.\n   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).\n   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.\n\n   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of\n   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.\n2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the\n   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing\n   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;\n   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.\n3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.\n\n**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed\n[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are\nimmutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the\npush force-updates `main`.\nThe standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*\nthe close-out push.\n\n### vc-x1 push wrapper\n\n`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See\n`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags.\n\n**Current limitation**: only fully supports the\n[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other\nshapes need manual jj steps. Please review.\"\n- **At Commit Description review** — present `$TITLE`\n  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.\n  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...\n  --body ...` invocation by default.\n- **At Post close-out review** — surface the shape\n  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;\n  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /\n  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.\n\n### After push or finalize: stop and wait\n\nAfter you **push** (cross the remote boundary) or launch\n**finalize** on the `.claude` repo (`vc-x1 finalize --repo\n.claude --squash --push <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach`) — by\nhand or via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper — you **MUST NEVER**\nproceed (next step, edit, tool call, text output) until the\nuser explicitly directs you to continue. **Even when the next\nstep seems obvious — wait.** Treat push-or-finalize as a hard\nstop for the whole turn.\n\n`vc-x1 push` performs both as its tail stages — `push-app`\nthen the detached `vc-x1 finalize` on `.claude` — so there is\nno gap left to speak in once the push is invoked. Put **all**\nclosing words *before* invoking it; do not purposely emit anything\nafter the tool returns.\n\nWhy (`.claude` is the live journal finalize snapshots →\nsquashes → pushes):\n\n- **`--detach`**: lets the tool return immediately so the\n  harness can keep flushing the *trailing* session-data — the\n  tool call's own transcript and any words emitted *before*\n  the invoke — into the snapshot.\n- **`--delay 10`**: gives the harness time to complete that\n  flush before the snapshot is taken. It is **not** time for\n  the bot to do more work.\n- **silence**: the bot must not summarize or perform any work\n  after the tool returns.\n\n**Known slip**: the bot has emitted a summary after launching\nfinalize. There is no \"harmless\" closing line — if it's worth\nsaying, say it *before* the invoke.\n\n### Recovery\n\n- **If push exits before `finalize-claude`** (e.g.\n  failure between `push-app` and `finalize-claude`), run\n  finalize by hand:\n\n  ```\n  vc-x1 finalize --repo .claude --squash --push <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach --log /tmp/vc-x1-finalize.log\n  ```\n\n- **Run finalize again if `@` is non-empty** after the\n  finalize's squash-and-commit (also desirable after\n  extra activity by the bot's agents).\n  - Why: finalize snapshots `.claude` at `--delay`, but the\n    bot keeps writing session data while it runs — the tool's\n    own invocation plus the bot's closing response land\n    *after* the snapshot.\n  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a\n    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could\n    change; it is not under the user's control.)\n  - Fix: run `vc-x1 finalize --repo .claude --squash --push\n    <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach` another time to capture\n    that tail; one extra pass is generally enough.\n    - Verified 0.64.0: two finalizes were executed and\n      we purposely used the bot again and the second finalize\n      captured everything.\n  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave\n    `@` non-empty — e.g. the bot's back end may decide to\n    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes\n    and land after the snapshot. The remedy is the same: just\n    run finalize again. This is why a single pass is never\n    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.\n- **Clear push's saved state** after any out-of-band\n  recovery — `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml` or `vc-x1 push\n  <bookmark> --restart` — otherwise push resumes from a\n  stale stage.\n- **Late code-repo tweak after `push-app` succeeded**\n  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj\n  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a\n  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any\n  push.\n\n## ochid trailers\n\nA **chid** is jj's change ID — a permanent identifier\nthat survives rebases and describes (see\n[`jj-revsets.md`](jj-revsets.md)). An **ochid** trailer\non a commit body links it to its counterpart in the\nother repo via that counterpart's chid, written as a\nworkspace-root-relative path. See\n[`forks-multi-user.md`](forks-multi-user.md) for the\nmulti-line trailer design (multi-user / forking).\n\n- **Code-side commits** each carry one\n  `ochid: /.claude/<.claude-chid>` — the `.claude`\n  change ID.\n- **The `.claude` commit** has one `ochid: /<code-chid>`\n  per code commit in that push. More than one occurs on\n  Merge non-ff close-out (one ochid per Work commit in\n  the cycle).\n\nUse `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to capture the change\nIDs (first line app, second `.claude`).\n\n## Iterative work\n\nWhen work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits\nfrom incremental review, loop:\n\n1. `jj new -R .` — fresh empty `@` on top of the target.\n2. Make the next round of changes.\n3. User reviews the round (see\n   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).\n4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a\n   new empty `@`.\n5. If not done, go to step 2.\n\nSame jj mechanics as a\n[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at\nsingle-commit scope — the cycle's version suffix\ndoesn't change.\n\n## Sub-cycle ladders\n\nWhen a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see\n[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work\ncommits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and\n**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the\nparent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch —\nfor review and bisection only.\n\n### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder\n\nFor each Work commit in the ladder:\n\n1. `jj new -R .` — create a fresh empty `@`.\n2. Do the commit's work.\n3. Run `cargo test --bins`. **Non-negotiable** — build\n   and clippy alone miss regressions until a later\n   commit runs the full suite, raising bisection cost.\n4. `jj describe -m \"...\" -m \"...\" -R .` — working title\n   only (no version suffix); the sub-cycle Close-out\n   collects everything into one final commit with the\n   `(X.Y.Z-N)` marker.\n\n### Navigating the ladder\n\nCommon moves:\n\n- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .` — see the whole ladder\n  from its base.\n- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .` — jump `@` to any ladder\n  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.\n- `jj edit @-- -R .` — quick-jump back two commits.\n- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .` — review one commit in\n  isolation.\n\nModifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;\ndescendants auto-rebase.\n\n### Close-out: squash the ladder\n\nWhen all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:\n\n```\njj squash --from \"<base>..@-\" --into @ -u -R .\n```\n\n`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`\nkeeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.\nAfter squash, history is linear: `<base> → @`;\nintermediate commits are auto-abandoned.\n\nThen `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.\n\nFor N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty\nwhen `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.\n\n### Recovery\n\nIf a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing\nprior commits:\n\n- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`\n  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same\n  parent.\n- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,\n  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`\n  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.\n- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows\n  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts\n  to that point. Full undo — removes *all* ladder work\n  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.\n\n# References\n\n- [`jj-revsets.md`](jj-revsets.md) — revset primitives\n  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).\n- [`forks-multi-user.md`](forks-multi-user.md) — multi-ochid\n  trailer design (fork / multi-user generalization).\n- [`substep-test.sh`](substep-test.sh) — script that\n  scaffolds a 4-revision ladder under `/tmp/substep-test`\n  for squash-recipe experiments.\n- 0.41.1-6.5 cycle — first multi-commit ladder usage. /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1-work-repo-template/.claude/e5ec0e9d-b1c8-4143-a844-c6e520a1770b.jsonl:105:{"parentUuid":"e983fe1f-9326-441b-929e-a5f022e982e4","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"895b5e56-f3a5-4114-8df0-8a10b3e56c75","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01HBr29cKSjbSju3Dqyagpzq","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Forking and multi-user coordination\n2\t\n3\tCaptures design discussion about two related but separable\n4\tconcerns:\n5\t\n6\t1. **Forking** a dual-repo workspace — working on an older\n7\t   code-side base while keeping the bot side append-only.\n8\t2. **Multi-user collaboration** on the same dual-repo —\n9\t   multiple humans, multiple bot sessions, code-side merges.\n10\t\n11\tBoth surface the same underlying tension: the code repo has\n12\tthe classic git/jj DAG (branches, merges, rebases), while the\n13\tbot repo is fundamentally an append-only journal of\n14\tconversations that should never be rewritten.\n15\t\n16\tFor the *content* of the bot repo (vendor identity, format\n17\tversioning, multi-bot conventions, vendor-subdir directory\n18\tlayout), see the companion file\n19\t[`bot-data-formats.md`](bot-data-formats.md).\n20\t\n21\tThis file is forward-looking: most of what it describes is\n22\tthe bot thinks, not implemented. Treat as a design reference,\n23\tnot a status doc.\n24\t\n25\t## Forking with the bot side staying linear\n26\t\n27\t### The asymmetric situation\n28\t\n29\tWhen work needs to happen on an older code-side base — e.g.,\n30\t0.41.1 work branched off 0.41.0 while 0.42.0 is in flight on\n31\tmain — the code repo can fork without difficulty. That's a\n32\tnormal git/jj branch.\n33\t\n34\tThe bot repo can't fork the same way: each session is a linear\n35\tconversation, and rewriting an existing session line would\n36\tfalsify the historical record. The conversation that happened\n37\tis the conversation that happened; it doesn't get re-played\n38\tfrom a different branch base.\n39\t\n40\t### chid stability across rebase\n41\t\n42\tjj's two-id model is built for this scenario. Each commit has\n43\tboth:\n44\t\n45\t- `commit_id` — git SHA, changes on rewrite.\n46\t- `change_id` — stable across `describe` / `rebase` /\n47\t  `squash-into-self`.\n48\t\n49\t`ochid:` trailers carry change_ids. So when a code-side branch\n50\tlater rebases on top of another branch, change_ids are\n51\tpreserved and ochid trailers in both directions still resolve.\n52\t\n53\tThe bot thinks the only operations that break this are\n54\t`jj squash` (folding two commits into one — collapses two\n55\tchange_ids into one) and `jj abandon` (removing a commit —\n56\tloses the change_id entirely). Pure rebase is safe.\n57\t\n58\t### Why not time-based linkers\n59\t\n60\tTime isn't a stronger primitive than change_id:\n61\t\n62\t- Clock skew between processes / repos breaks ordering.\n63\t- Time still doesn't survive rewrites any better than\n64\t  change_id does — you'd still need a stable identifier baked\n65\t  into the trailer that matches some property of the\n66\t  counterpart commit.\n67\t- change_id is jj's intended stability primitive — that's\n68\t  literally the job it exists to do.\n69\t\n70\tIf the change_id scheme ever shows weakness, the bot thinks\n71\tthe answer is jj-side hygiene (don't `squash`-collapse during\n72\trebase) rather than switching primitives.\n73\t\n74\t### Partner bookmarks\n75\t\n76\tThe chosen technique for forking the code side while keeping\n77\tthe bot side linear: **partner bookmarks**.\n78\t\n79\tWhen a code-side branch needs to advance independently, create\n80\ta bookmark of the same name on the bot side starting at the\n81\t*current* bot HEAD — not at the historical bot commit paired\n82\twith the code-side branch base. The two bookmarks share a name\n83\tand advance together via `vc-x1 push`, but each carries its\n84\town repo's state.\n85\t\n86\tOther names considered and rejected:\n87\t\n88\t- **mirror** — implies symmetric content. The bookmarks are\n89\t  not mirrors; they hold different content with no\n90\t  point-by-point correspondence.\n91\t- **tandem** — captures cooperation, but slightly less common\n92\t  in software vocabulary.\n93\t- **paired** — bland; \"pair\" can imply matching halves.\n94\t- **disjoint** / **asymmetric** — describe a property of the\n95\t  relationship, not a label for the technique.\n96\t- **yoked** — accurate metaphor but obscure.\n97\t\n98\t**partner** won because it conveys cooperation without\n99\timplying duplication. Always subject to change as we live\n100\twith the term.\n101\t\n102\tThe asymmetric ordering between code and bot history (rebased\n103\tmain commits on the code side will eventually point at bot\n104\tcommits that come *before* their partner-branch pairs in bot\n105\thistory) is a cosmetic wrinkle, not a correctness problem —\n106\tchange_ids resolve regardless of position.\n107\t\n108\t### Recovery anchor\n109\t\n110\tThe original main HEAD — the commit being \"branched away\n111\tfrom\" — should stay put, not be rewritten or rewound. It's\n112\tthe recovery anchor for the operation. If the partner-branch\n113\twork goes wrong, main is still where it was, and recovery is\n114\t`jj abandon` on the new branch's commits.\n115\t\n116\tIn the 0.41.1 init+clone refactor, this means main stays at\n117\tits current 0.42.0-4 docs-capture commit (`55eadc8`) for the\n118\tduration of the side-branch work. That commit becomes\n119\tredundant after the eventual rebase — its content has been\n120\tre-landed on `init-clone-refactor` — and gets dropped during\n121\tthe rebase rather than being rewound now.\n122\t\n123\t## Multi-user collaboration\n124\t\n125\tThe bot thinks the same model — linear forest on the bot\n126\tside, multi-trailer reconciliation on the code side —\n127\tgeneralizes naturally to multi-user.\n128\t\n129\t### Bot repo as a forest of linear chains\n130\t\n131\tEach session is one append-only chain. The bot repo is a\n132\tforest of those chains; never merged. No bot-side merge\n133\tcommits at all. Code-side has a DAG (merges, branches);\n134\tbot-side is a forest. The mapping is the multi-ochid trailer\n135\tset on each code commit, fanning out to the contributing\n136\tchain tips.\n137\t\n138\tThe bot thinks this is cleaner than \"bot side mirrors code\n139\tside topology\" because:\n140\t\n141\t- Each conversation is a wire-format record of what was\n142\t  actually said. Merging two conversations into one commit\n143\t  would falsify that record.\n144\t- \"Never rewrite bot commits\" becomes an enforceable rule —\n145\t  change_ids on the bot side are automatically stable.\n146\t- Storage and sync stay simple — appending only, no merge\n147\t  conflict resolution on the bot side ever.\n148\t\n149\t### Multi-line ochid trailer\n150\t\n151\tStandard git trailer convention allows multiple values for\n152\tthe same key. Just emit `ochid:` once per pointer:\n153\t\n154\t```\n155\tochid: /.claude/abc123\n156\tochid: /.claude/def456\n157\tochid: /.claude/ghi789\n158\t```\n159\t\n160\tSingle-pointer commits stay backward compatible — they're\n161\tjust the N=1 case. No version bump needed; existing parsers\n162\teither already accept repeated trailers or are easy to\n163\textend.\n164\t\n165\t### When multi-ochid actually applies\n166\t\n167\t- **Code-side merge with no extra bot work** — N ochids =\n168\t  the merge parents' contributing tip change_ids (one per\n169\t  parent). Possibly with de-duplication if parents share\n170\t  ancestry.\n171\t- **Code-side merge with conflict-resolution session** —\n172\t  N parents' ochids + the resolution session's tip ochid.\n173\t  If user A and user B merge into M and user C resolves the\n174\t  conflict, M has 3 ochids: A's tip, B's tip, C's session\n175\t  tip.\n176\t- **Single-user single-session** — still 1 ochid. Same as\n177\t  today.\n178\t- **Code rebase** — ochids unchanged (change_ids are\n179\t  stable). Same as today. Multi-user rebases work the same\n180\t  as single-user.\n181\t\n182\t### Staged fork integration\n183\t\n184\tHow a contributed cycle's worth of changes enters a\n185\tdownstream repo, keeping the as-is record separate from the\n186\tintegration work:\n187\t\n188\t- **As-is acceptance.** A contributed set of changes lands\n189\t  first in a dedicated branch *exactly as submitted* — no\n190\t  merge, no squash, no tweak. The contributor's `ochid:`\n191\t  trailers are preserved verbatim; the branch is a faithful\n192\t  record of what was contributed.\n193\t- **Integration as separate steps.** Merging, squashing, or\n194\t  tweaking that work onto the target line happens\n195\t  afterward, as one or more separate steps on an\n196\t  intermediate branch. Each is its own cycle and may add\n197\t  its own bot session.\n198\t- **Resulting ochid set.** An integrated commit therefore\n199\t  carries a *set* of ochids — the contributor's original\n200\t  pointer(s) plus any integration-session pointer(s): the\n201\t  [multi-line ochid trailer](#multi-line-ochid-trailer)\n202\t  applied to the fork case rather than the octopus-merge\n203\t  case.\n204\t\n205\tThe contributing bot repos live in different locations\n206\t(different users, different remotes), so each ochid in the\n207\tset must name *which* bot repo as well as the chid. Three\n208\trepresentations, in increasing indirection:\n209\t\n210\t- **Workspace-relative path** — `/.claude/<chid>`,\n211\t  `/.claude-alice/<chid>`. Today's form; resolves only\n212\t  repos under the local workspace root.\n213\t- **Full URL** — `https://github.com/alice/bot#<chid>`\n214\t  (see [Per-user bot repos via URL-shaped\n215\t  ochid](#per-user-bot-repos-via-url-shaped-ochid)).\n216\t  Self-contained, no external table; verbose, exposed to\n217\t  link rot.\n218\t- **`.vc-config.toml` repo index** — a tuple\n219\t  `(repo-index, chid)` where `repo-index` keys a\n220\t  repo-location table declared once in `.vc-config.toml`.\n221\t  The trailer stays short, and relocating a repo is a\n222\t  one-line config edit instead of rewriting every trailer.\n223\t  Cost: indirection — the trailer is meaningless without\n224\t  the config, so a commit inspected outside its workspace\n225\t  (a raw `git show` elsewhere) can't resolve it.\n226\t\n227\tThe bot thinks index and URL forms are complementary, not\n228\trivals — index for repos the project already tracks in\n229\t`.vc-config.toml`, URL for one-off external contributors —\n230\tand a resolver accepting all three (path, URL, index) is\n231\tthe one-rule dispatch the URL-shaped section already\n232\tdescribes, with a third arm.\n233\t\n234\t### Per-user vs shared bot repo\n235\t\n236\tOpen question worth deciding before code lands.\n237\t\n238\t- **Shared bot repo** (today's model extended): one\n239\t  `.claude/` repo holds all sessions across all users. Push\n240\t  from any user appends a chain. Pros: viewer sees\n241\t  everything in one place; cross-references resolve locally.\n242\t  Cons: every user pulls every other user's session data on\n243\t  sync — could be heavy. Permissions are coarse.\n244\t- **Per-user bot repos**: each user has their own\n245\t  `.claude-<user>/` repo, ochid trailers carry a user\n246\t  qualifier (`ochid: /.claude-alice/abc123`). Pros:\n247\t  lightweight sync, natural permissions. Cons: viewer needs\n248\t  to know all the bot-repo URLs to show full context;\n249\t  offline viewing breaks if you don't have the relevant\n250\t  user's repo.\n251\t\n252\tThe bot thinks **shared** is the default with a per-project\n253\tescape hatch — most teams want the cross-references to\n254\t\"just work.\" The qualifier in ochid (the path component\n255\tafter the leading `/`) already encodes either model:\n256\t`/.claude/<chid>` for shared, `/.claude-alice/<chid>` for\n257\tper-user. The trailer format itself is forward-compatible.\n258\t\n259\t### Per-user bot repos via URL-shaped ochid\n260\t\n261\tPer-user bot repos become practical for distributed\n262\tprojects (open-source, multi-org) when ochid trailers can\n263\tqualify by URL rather than only workspace-relative path.\n264\tThis generalizes the per-user model in the section above\n265\tfrom \"co-located teams sharing a workspace\" to \"anyone on\n266\tthe public internet.\"\n267\t\n268\t**Trailer shape.** Existing path form is\n269\tworkspace-root-relative (`/.claude/<chid>` for shared,\n270\t`/.claude-alice/<chid>` for per-user-in-shared-workspace).\n271\tURL form generalizes the qualifier to a remote repo:\n272\t\n273\t```\n274\tochid: https://github.com/alice/bot-sessions#<chid>\n275\tochid: git@github.com:alice/bot-sessions.git#<chid>\n276\t```\n277\t\n278\tParser dispatch is one rule: if the qualifier parses as a\n279\tURL, fetch over the network; otherwise resolve relative\n280\tto workspace root. Existing path-form trailers stay the\n281\tN=1 backward-compatible case. No schema versioning\n282\tneeded.\n283\t\n284\t**Link rot is the load-bearing problem.** A contributor\n285\tcan publish their bot repo, get merged, then later make\n286\tit private or delete it. The ochid URL 404s; bot context\n287\tis lost. The bot thinks this is a real-but-not-\n288\tcatastrophic leak — the commit's code and\n289\t`Signed-off-by:` line remain authoritative; bot context\n290\tis a nice-to-have for understanding patch development,\n291\tnot a load-bearing semantic. Direct analogue: dead URLs\n292\tin academic citations, mailing-list links in older\n293\tkernel commit messages. Annoying for archaeology, not\n294\tfatal.\n295\t\n296\t**Mitigations, in order of practical adoption:**\n297\t\n298\t1. **Project-side mirroring at merge time.** When a\n299\t   maintainer accepts a PR, project tooling fetches the\n300\t   contributor's bot repo at the referenced chid and\n301\t   mirrors to a project-namespace archive (e.g.\n302\t   `bot-archives/<contributor>-<date>-<chid>.jsonl`).\n303\t   Future ochid resolution falls back to the mirror if\n304\t   the original URL 404s. The bot thinks this is the\n305\t   only mitigation most projects would actually adopt —\n306\t   cheap, obvious upside, no friction for contributors.\n307\t   Same pattern as LKML's permanent archive.\n308\t2. **Cryptographic stapling.** Embed a hash of the bot\n309\t   repo's tip at submission time:\n310\t   `ochid: <url>#<chid>;sha256=<hash>`. Tamper-detection\n311\t   stays sound even if retrieval fails; doesn't recover\n312\t   data. Adds maintenance burden to trailer parsing.\n313\t3. **CI-enforced live ochid at merge.** Project CI\n314\t   fetches the URL, verifies it resolves with parseable\n315\t   content, before allowing merge. Doesn't prevent\n316\t   later lock/delete but ensures the merge moment was\n317\t   sound. Contentious in open-source culture (gates\n318\t   contributors on infra they don't own).\n319\t\n320\t**Opt-out via project policy.** A no-bot-context commit\n321\tisn't a leak — it's a project policy choice. A project\n322\tthat wants bot transparency mandates each commit carry\n323\t≥1 `ochid:` trailer or an explicit\n324\t`No-bot-context: <reason>` trailer. Enforceable in CI,\n325\tidentical pattern to existing `Signed-off-by:`.\n326\tContributors who want privacy decline that project's\n327\tcontribution norms; their commits go elsewhere or omit\n328\tthe trailer where the project allows.\n329\t\n330\t**Cross-bot interop bonus.** Once URL-shaped, the\n331\ttrailer doesn't have to point at a Claude Code repo.\n332\tCodex, Cursor, Aider, custom in-house tools — anyone\n333\twhose bot leaves a publishable session record can host\n334\ttheir own bot repo and emit ochid trailers in the same\n335\tformat. The trailer becomes \"where to find the AI\n336\tsession that produced this commit,\" not \"where to find\n337\tthe Claude Code session.\" Strictly bigger ecosystem\n338\tplay with no extra design cost.\n339\t\n340\t**Implication for shared-central scaling.** URL-shaped\n341\tper-user repos potentially short-circuit the\n342\tsize/threshold problem documented below. Each\n343\tcontributor pays for their own bot repo; project pays\n344\tfor an opt-in mirror archive sized per its policy. The\n345\t\"50 devs share one ~15G bot repo\" problem becomes \"50\n346\tdevs each maintain their own ~300M bot repo, project\n347\tmirrors selectively.\"\n348\t\n349\tTrade-off: shared-central keeps cross-references local\n350\tand fast; per-user-via-URL needs a network fetch (or a\n351\twarm mirror) to resolve any non-local trailer. Pick by\n352\tproject shape — small co-located teams favor shared;\n353\tdistributed open-source favors per-user-via-URL.\n354\t\n355\t### Bot-side commit immutability\n356\t\n357\tCodify \"never rewrite bot commits\" as a hard rule. The\n358\treason: change_ids on the bot side need to be permanently\n359\tstable for ochid trailers from the code side to resolve\n360\tforever. Even `jj describe` (description-only) changes the\n361\tcommit_id, which doesn't break change_ids but does signal\n362\tthat bot commits are mutable in a way they shouldn't be.\n363\t\n364\tTrade: any commit-level metadata fix has to be done by\n365\tappending a new commit, not amending the existing one.\n366\tAwkward but correct.\n367\t\n368\t### Bot-repo size and scaling thresholds\n369\t\n370\tConcrete measurement on a single-developer vc-x1 project\n371\t(2026-05-07, after `cargo clean`):\n372\t\n373\t- Code repo (excluding `.claude`): ~4M\n374\t- Bot repo (`.claude`): 311M\n375\t- Ratio: ~78:1 bot-to-code\n376\t\n377\tCause: every Claude Code session writes a UUID-named\n378\t`.jsonl` file. Content is mostly unique per session —\n379\tgit/jj packs each file's append history well, but\n380\tcross-file dedup is weak. So bot-repo bytes scale roughly\n381\tlinearly with total session count.\n382\t\n383\tLinear extrapolation to shared-central multi-user (the bot\n384\tthinks this is a reasonable upper bound; actual savings\n385\tfrom cross-session dedup are small):\n386\t\n387\t- 5 devs: ~1.5G\n388\t- 20 devs: ~6G\n389\t- 50 devs: ~15G\n390\t\n391\tRough operational thresholds:\n392\t\n393\t- **≤ ~10 users:** shared-central is fine.\n394\t- **~10-50 users:** shared-central starts hurting\n395\t  (multi-minute initial clone; noticeable `vc-x1 sync`\n396\t  pulls).\n397\t- **> ~50 users or > ~10G bot repo:** mitigations become\n398\t  necessary.\n399\t\n400\t### Monotonic-growth asymmetry\n401\t\n402\tBot-repo size only grows. Once a session jsonl is\n403\tcommitted, the bot-side immutability rule keeps it\n404\tforever. This is by design (historical record), but it\n405\tmeans the bot repo has no analog of `cargo clean`:\n406\tcode-repo working bytes can be reclaimed (build artifacts\n407\tcome back on `cargo build`); bot-repo bytes are permanent.\n408\t\n409\tSizing assumptions for shared-central scaling are a\n410\tone-way ratchet, not a steady-state cost.\n411\t\n412\t### Mitigation menu (when thresholds approach)\n413\t\n414\tNone worth building preemptively. Listed so trigger points\n415\thave known responses:\n416\t\n417\t1. **Bot-repo pruning/archiving.** Move closed-out\n418\t   sessions (older than N months, or tied to commits no\n419\t   longer in any active branch) to an archive repo.\n420\t   Active bot repo stays small; archive fetched on demand\n421\t   when older history is referenced. The bot thinks this\n422\t   is the cheapest big win — recent sessions are the hot\n423\t   set, old ones are cold.\n424\t2. **Sparse fetch by trailer-referenced sessions.** When\n425\t   fetching the code repo, derive the set of bot-side\n426\t   change_ids referenced by ochids in the fetched range\n427\t   and fetch only those bot commits. Requires git/jj\n428\t   sparse-fetch + a trailer-walking step. Heavier to\n429\t   build but decouples clone cost from bot-repo size.\n430\t3. **Per-user bot repos.** The structural alternative —\n431\t   see \"Per-user vs shared bot repo\" above. Viable when\n432\t   shared-central pruning/sparse-fetch isn't enough.\n433\t4. **LFS for `.jsonl`.** Probably overkill — LFS targets\n434\t   binary blobs, not append-only text. Listed only\n435\t   because it's a known git escape hatch.\n436\t\n437\t### Tracking trigger\n438\t\n439\tConcretely measurable: the 311M baseline is the current\n440\tbenchmark. Treat as a design reference,\nnot a status doc.\n\n## Forking with the bot side staying linear\n\n### The asymmetric situation\n\nWhen work needs to happen on an older code-side base — e.g.,\n0.41.1 work branched off 0.41.0 while 0.42.0 is in flight on\nmain — the code repo can fork without difficulty. That's a\nnormal git/jj branch.\n\nThe bot repo can't fork the same way: each session is a linear\nconversation, and rewriting an existing session line would\nfalsify the historical record. The conversation that happened\nis the conversation that happened; it doesn't get re-played\nfrom a different branch base.\n\n### chid stability across rebase\n\njj's two-id model is built for this scenario. Each commit has\nboth:\n\n- `commit_id` — git SHA, changes on rewrite.\n- `change_id` — stable across `describe` / `rebase` /\n  `squash-into-self`.\n\n`ochid:` trailers carry change_ids. So when a code-side branch\nlater rebases on top of another branch, change_ids are\npreserved and ochid trailers in both directions still resolve.\n\nThe bot thinks the only operations that break this are\n`jj squash` (folding two commits into one — collapses two\nchange_ids into one) and `jj abandon` (removing a commit —\nloses the change_id entirely). Pure rebase is safe.\n\n### Why not time-based linkers\n\nTime isn't a stronger primitive than change_id:\n\n- Clock skew between processes / repos breaks ordering.\n- Time still doesn't survive rewrites any better than\n  change_id does — you'd still need a stable identifier baked\n  into the trailer that matches some property of the\n  counterpart commit.\n- change_id is jj's intended stability primitive — that's\n  literally the job it exists to do.\n\nIf the change_id scheme ever shows weakness, the bot thinks\nthe answer is jj-side hygiene (don't `squash`-collapse during\nrebase) rather than switching primitives.\n\n### Partner bookmarks\n\nThe chosen technique for forking the code side while keeping\nthe bot side linear: **partner bookmarks**.\n\nWhen a code-side branch needs to advance independently, create\na bookmark of the same name on the bot side starting at the\n*current* bot HEAD — not at the historical bot commit paired\nwith the code-side branch base. The two bookmarks share a name\nand advance together via `vc-x1 push`, but each carries its\nown repo's state.\n\nOther names considered and rejected:\n\n- **mirror** — implies symmetric content. The bookmarks are\n  not mirrors; they hold different content with no\n  point-by-point correspondence.\n- **tandem** — captures cooperation, but slightly less common\n  in software vocabulary.\n- **paired** — bland; \"pair\" can imply matching halves.\n- **disjoint** / **asymmetric** — describe a property of the\n  relationship, not a label for the technique.\n- **yoked** — accurate metaphor but obscure.\n\n**partner** won because it conveys cooperation without\nimplying duplication. Always subject to change as we live\nwith the term.\n\nThe asymmetric ordering between code and bot history (rebased\nmain commits on the code side will eventually point at bot\ncommits that come *before* their partner-branch pairs in bot\nhistory) is a cosmetic wrinkle, not a correctness problem —\nchange_ids resolve regardless of position.\n\n### Recovery anchor\n\nThe original main HEAD — the commit being \"branched away\nfrom\" — should stay put, not be rewritten or rewound. It's\nthe recovery anchor for the operation. If the partner-branch\nwork goes wrong, main is still where it was, and recovery is\n`jj abandon` on the new branch's commits.\n\nIn the 0.41.1 init+clone refactor, this means main stays at\nits current 0.42.0-4 docs-capture commit (`55eadc8`) for the\nduration of the side-branch work. That commit becomes\nredundant after the eventual rebase — its content has been\nre-landed on `init-clone-refactor` — and gets dropped during\nthe rebase rather than being rewound now.\n\n## Multi-user collaboration\n\nThe bot thinks the same model — linear forest on the bot\nside, multi-trailer reconciliation on the code side —\ngeneralizes naturally to multi-user.\n\n### Bot repo as a forest of linear chains\n\nEach session is one append-only chain. The bot repo is a\nforest of those chains; never merged. No bot-side merge\ncommits at all. Code-side has a DAG (merges, branches);\nbot-side is a forest. The mapping is the multi-ochid trailer\nset on each code commit, fanning out to the contributing\nchain tips.\n\nThe bot thinks this is cleaner than \"bot side mirrors code\nside topology\" because:\n\n- Each conversation is a wire-format record of what was\n  actually said. Merging two conversations into one commit\n  would falsify that record.\n- \"Never rewrite bot commits\" becomes an enforceable rule —\n  change_ids on the bot side are automatically stable.\n- Storage and sync stay simple — appending only, no merge\n  conflict resolution on the bot side ever.\n\n### Multi-line ochid trailer\n\nStandard git trailer convention allows multiple values for\nthe same key. Just emit `ochid:` once per pointer:\n\n```\nochid: /.claude/abc123\nochid: /.claude/def456\nochid: /.claude/ghi789\n```\n\nSingle-pointer commits stay backward compatible — they're\njust the N=1 case. No version bump needed; existing parsers\neither already accept repeated trailers or are easy to\nextend.\n\n### When multi-ochid actually applies\n\n- **Code-side merge with no extra bot work** — N ochids =\n  the merge parents' contributing tip change_ids (one per\n  parent). Possibly with de-duplication if parents share\n  ancestry.\n- **Code-side merge with conflict-resolution session** —\n  N parents' ochids + the resolution session's tip ochid.\n  If user A and user B merge into M and user C resolves the\n  conflict, M has 3 ochids: A's tip, B's tip, C's session\n  tip.\n- **Single-user single-session** — still 1 ochid. Same as\n  today.\n- **Code rebase** — ochids unchanged (change_ids are\n  stable). Same as today. Multi-user rebases work the same\n  as single-user.\n\n### Staged fork integration\n\nHow a contributed cycle's worth of changes enters a\ndownstream repo, keeping the as-is record separate from the\nintegration work:\n\n- **As-is acceptance.** A contributed set of changes lands\n  first in a dedicated branch *exactly as submitted* — no\n  merge, no squash, no tweak. The contributor's `ochid:`\n  trailers are preserved verbatim; the branch is a faithful\n  record of what was contributed.\n- **Integration as separate steps.** Merging, squashing, or\n  tweaking that work onto the target line happens\n  afterward, as one or more separate steps on an\n  intermediate branch. Each is its own cycle and may add\n  its own bot session.\n- **Resulting ochid set.** An integrated commit therefore\n  carries a *set* of ochids — the contributor's original\n  pointer(s) plus any integration-session pointer(s): the\n  [multi-line ochid trailer](#multi-line-ochid-trailer)\n  applied to the fork case rather than the octopus-merge\n  case.\n\nThe contributing bot repos live in different locations\n(different users, different remotes), so each ochid in the\nset must name *which* bot repo as well as the chid. Three\nrepresentations, in increasing indirection:\n\n- **Workspace-relative path** — `/.claude/<chid>`,\n  `/.claude-alice/<chid>`. Today's form; resolves only\n  repos under the local workspace root.\n- **Full URL** — `https://github.com/alice/bot#<chid>`\n  (see [Per-user bot repos via URL-shaped\n  ochid](#per-user-bot-repos-via-url-shaped-ochid)).\n  Self-contained, no external table; verbose, exposed to\n  link rot.\n- **`.vc-config.toml` repo index** — a tuple\n  `(repo-index, chid)` where `repo-index` keys a\n  repo-location table declared once in `.vc-config.toml`.\n  The trailer stays short, and relocating a repo is a\n  one-line config edit instead of rewriting every trailer.\n  Cost: indirection — the trailer is meaningless without\n  the config, so a commit inspected outside its workspace\n  (a raw `git show` elsewhere) can't resolve it.\n\nThe bot thinks index and URL forms are complementary, not\nrivals — index for repos the project already tracks in\n`.vc-config.toml`, URL for one-off external contributors —\nand a resolver accepting all three (path, URL, index) is\nthe one-rule dispatch the URL-shaped section already\ndescribes, with a third arm.\n\n### Per-user vs shared bot repo\n\nOpen question worth deciding before code lands.\n\n- **Shared bot repo** (today's model extended): one\n  `.claude/` repo holds all sessions across all users. Push\n  from any user appends a chain. Pros: viewer sees\n  everything in one place; cross-references resolve locally.\n  Cons: every user pulls every other user's session data on\n  sync — could be heavy. Permissions are coarse.\n- **Per-user bot repos**: each user has their own\n  `.claude-<user>/` repo, ochid trailers carry a user\n  qualifier (`ochid: /.claude-alice/abc123`). Pros:\n  lightweight sync, natural permissions. Cons: viewer needs\n  to know all the bot-repo URLs to show full context;\n  offline viewing breaks if you don't have the relevant\n  user's repo.\n\nThe bot thinks **shared** is the default with a per-project\nescape hatch — most teams want the cross-references to\n\"just work.\" The qualifier in ochid (the path component\nafter the leading `/`) already encodes either model:\n`/.claude/<chid>` for shared, `/.claude-alice/<chid>` for\nper-user. The trailer format itself is forward-compatible.\n\n### Per-user bot repos via URL-shaped ochid\n\nPer-user bot repos become practical for distributed\nprojects (open-source, multi-org) when ochid trailers can\nqualify by URL rather than only workspace-relative path.\nThis generalizes the per-user model in the section above\nfrom \"co-located teams sharing a workspace\" to \"anyone on\nthe public internet.\"\n\n**Trailer shape.** Existing path form is\nworkspace-root-relative (`/.claude/<chid>` for shared,\n`/.claude-alice/<chid>` for per-user-in-shared-workspace).\nURL form generalizes the qualifier to a remote repo:\n\n```\nochid: https://github.com/alice/bot-sessions#<chid>\nochid: git@github.com:alice/bot-sessions.git#<chid>\n```\n\nParser dispatch is one rule: if the qualifier parses as a\nURL, fetch over the network; otherwise resolve relative\nto workspace root. Existing path-form trailers stay the\nN=1 backward-compatible case. No schema versioning\nneeded.\n\n**Link rot is the load-bearing problem.** A contributor\ncan publish their bot repo, get merged, then later make\nit private or delete it. The ochid URL 404s; bot context\nis lost. The bot thinks this is a real-but-not-\ncatastrophic leak — the commit's code and\n`Signed-off-by:` line remain authoritative; bot context\nis a nice-to-have for understanding patch development,\nnot a load-bearing semantic. Direct analogue: dead URLs\nin academic citations, mailing-list links in older\nkernel commit messages. Annoying for archaeology, not\nfatal.\n\n**Mitigations, in order of practical adoption:**\n\n1. **Project-side mirroring at merge time.** When a\n   maintainer accepts a PR, project tooling fetches the\n   contributor's bot repo at the referenced chid and\n   mirrors to a project-namespace archive (e.g.\n   `bot-archives/<contributor>-<date>-<chid>.jsonl`).\n   Future ochid resolution falls back to the mirror if\n   the original URL 404s. The bot thinks this is the\n   only mitigation most projects would actually adopt —\n   cheap, obvious upside, no friction for contributors.\n   Same pattern as LKML's permanent archive.\n2. **Cryptographic stapling.** Embed a hash of the bot\n   repo's tip at submission time:\n   `ochid: <url>#<chid>;sha256=<hash>`. Tamper-detection\n   stays sound even if retrieval fails; doesn't recover\n   data. Adds maintenance burden to trailer parsing.\n3. **CI-enforced live ochid at merge.** Project CI\n   fetches the URL, verifies it resolves with parseable\n   content, before allowing merge. Doesn't prevent\n   later lock/delete but ensures the merge moment was\n   sound. Contentious in open-source culture (gates\n   contributors on infra they don't own).\n\n**Opt-out via project policy.** A no-bot-context commit\nisn't a leak — it's a project policy choice. A project\nthat wants bot transparency mandates each commit carry\n≥1 `ochid:` trailer or an explicit\n`No-bot-context: <reason>` trailer. Enforceable in CI,\nidentical pattern to existing `Signed-off-by:`.\nContributors who want privacy decline that project's\ncontribution norms; their commits go elsewhere or omit\nthe trailer where the project allows.\n\n**Cross-bot interop bonus.** Once URL-shaped, the\ntrailer doesn't have to point at a Claude Code repo.\nCodex, Cursor, Aider, custom in-house tools — anyone\nwhose bot leaves a publishable session record can host\ntheir own bot repo and emit ochid trailers in the same\nformat. The trailer becomes \"where to find the AI\nsession that produced this commit,\" not \"where to find\nthe Claude Code session.\" Strictly bigger ecosystem\nplay with no extra design cost.\n\n**Implication for shared-central scaling.** URL-shaped\nper-user repos potentially short-circuit the\nsize/threshold problem documented below. Each\ncontributor pays for their own bot repo; project pays\nfor an opt-in mirror archive sized per its policy. The\n\"50 devs share one ~15G bot repo\" problem becomes \"50\ndevs each maintain their own ~300M bot repo, project\nmirrors selectively.\"\n\nTrade-off: shared-central keeps cross-references local\nand fast; per-user-via-URL needs a network fetch (or a\nwarm mirror) to resolve any non-local trailer. Pick by\nproject shape — small co-located teams favor shared;\ndistributed open-source favors per-user-via-URL.\n\n### Bot-side commit immutability\n\nCodify \"never rewrite bot commits\" as a hard rule. The\nreason: change_ids on the bot side need to be permanently\nstable for ochid trailers from the code side to resolve\nforever. Even `jj describe` (description-only) changes the\ncommit_id, which doesn't break change_ids but does signal\nthat bot commits are mutable in a way they shouldn't be.\n\nTrade: any commit-level metadata fix has to be done by\nappending a new commit, not amending the existing one.\nAwkward but correct.\n\n### Bot-repo size and scaling thresholds\n\nConcrete measurement on a single-developer vc-x1 project\n(2026-05-07, after `cargo clean`):\n\n- Code repo (excluding `.claude`): ~4M\n- Bot repo (`.claude`): 311M\n- Ratio: ~78:1 bot-to-code\n\nCause: every Claude Code session writes a UUID-named\n`.jsonl` file. Content is mostly unique per session —\ngit/jj packs each file's append history well, but\ncross-file dedup is weak. So bot-repo bytes scale roughly\nlinearly with total session count.\n\nLinear extrapolation to shared-central multi-user (the bot\nthinks this is a reasonable upper bound; actual savings\nfrom cross-session dedup are small):\n\n- 5 devs: ~1.5G\n- 20 devs: ~6G\n- 50 devs: ~15G\n\nRough operational thresholds:\n\n- **≤ ~10 users:** shared-central is fine.\n- **~10-50 users:** shared-central starts hurting\n  (multi-minute initial clone; noticeable `vc-x1 sync`\n  pulls).\n- **> ~50 users or > ~10G bot repo:** mitigations become\n  necessary.\n\n### Monotonic-growth asymmetry\n\nBot-repo size only grows. Once a session jsonl is\ncommitted, the bot-side immutability rule keeps it\nforever. This is by design (historical record), but it\nmeans the bot repo has no analog of `cargo clean`:\ncode-repo working bytes can be reclaimed (build artifacts\ncome back on `cargo build`); bot-repo bytes are permanent.\n\nSizing assumptions for shared-central scaling are a\none-way ratchet, not a steady-state cost.\n\n### Mitigation menu (when thresholds approach)\n\nNone worth building preemptively. Listed so trigger points\nhave known responses:\n\n1. **Bot-repo pruning/archiving.** Move closed-out\n   sessions (older than N months, or tied to commits no\n   longer in any active branch) to an archive repo.\n   Active bot repo stays small; archive fetched on demand\n   when older history is referenced. The bot thinks this\n   is the cheapest big win — recent sessions are the hot\n   set, old ones are cold.\n2. **Sparse fetch by trailer-referenced sessions.** When\n   fetching the code repo, derive the set of bot-side\n   change_ids referenced by ochids in the fetched range\n   and fetch only those bot commits. Requires git/jj\n   sparse-fetch + a trailer-walking step. Heavier to\n   build but decouples clone cost from bot-repo size.\n3. **Per-user bot repos.** The structural alternative —\n   see \"Per-user vs shared bot repo\" above. Viable when\n   shared-central pruning/sparse-fetch isn't enough.\n4. **LFS for `.jsonl`.** Probably overkill — LFS targets\n   binary blobs, not append-only text. Listed only\n   because it's a known git escape hatch.\n\n### Tracking trigger\n\nConcretely measurable: the 311M baseline is the current\nbenchmark. When the shared-central bot repo crosses ~1G\nor starts dominating clone time noticeably, that's the\ndesign trigger for pruning. User count alone is not the\nright signal; bot-repo size is.\n\n## Future-direction notes\n\nTwo alternatives to the partner-bookmark technique that may\nbe worth considering once we live with the current scheme:\n\n### Always keep the bot repo on main\n\nInstead of creating a partner bookmark on the bot side for\neach code-side branch, the bot side could be locked to a\nsingle bookmark — `main` — for the entire lifetime of the\nproject. Every push would advance bot main, regardless of\nwhat bookmark the code side is on.\n\nThe bot thinks this aligns with \"bot history is one linear\njournal\" more strongly than partner bookmarks do. Partner\nbookmarks introduce *parallel* bot bookmarks even though the\nbot history under them is still linear; an always-main\ndiscipline removes that parallelism entirely.\n\nTrade: requires push / finalize / sync to support asymmetric\nbookmark names per side (see next note).\n\n### Multi-bookmark-name support in push / finalize / sync\n\nToday, `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` advances the same bookmark\nname on both code and bot sides. The \"always-on-main\"\ndiscipline above (and other asymmetric workflows) requires\npush / finalize / sync to take separate bookmark arguments\nper side, e.g.:\n\n```\nvc-x1 push --code-bookmark init-clone-refactor --bot-bookmark main\nvc-x1 push -B init-clone-refactor              # bot defaults to main\nvc-x1 push init-clone-refactor                  # both, today's behavior\n```\n\nThe bot thinks the right shape lands once `--scope` is\nfully wired across the dual-repo commands — `--scope`\nalready handles \"which side does this command apply to,\"\nand adding per-side bookmark arguments is a natural\nextension.\n\n## Open questions worth thinking about\n\n- **Conflict resolution sessions: how do they get\n  authored?** When user C resolves a merge conflict, does\n  their bot session start a fresh chain rooted \"from\n  nowhere,\" or branch off one of the contributing chains?\n  The chain-rooting question affects how the viewer renders\n  it.\n- **De-duplication on octopus merges.** If parents share\n  ancestry, you'll get redundant ochids. Trim to unique\n  tips? Keep all? The bot thinks trim, but worth deciding.\n- **Bot-side bookmark scheme.** Per-session bookmark?\n  Per-user-per-feature? Naming convention matters because\n  bookmarks are how `jj git push` decides what to send.\n- **Viewer concerns.** \"Show me the sessions that\n  contributed to this commit\" is straightforward (read the\n  trailers, walk back in each chain to the relevant range).\n  \"Show me the code commits this session contributed to\" is\n  the inverse and needs an index, since change_ids don't\n  carry forward references. required;\n5\tplain `cargo install --path .` is unsafe.\n6\t\n7\t## What we hit\n8\t\n9\tOn a clean worktree (after `rustup update` + `cargo clean`),\n10\t`cargo install --path .` failed inside `gix-object 0.58.0`:\n11\t\n12\t```\n13\terror[E0308]: mismatched types\n14\t  --> gix-object-0.58.0/src/parse.rs:72:5\n15\t   |\n16\t71 | ) -> ModalResult<gix_actor::SignatureRef<'a>, E> {\n17\t72 |
